articles.content:
CAA chief Bryan Lourd is urging the full Congress to pass the No Fakes Act and deliver it to President Trump for signature, a move Lourd says would protect everyone, famous or not, from nonconsensual digital replicas of their voices and likenesses.

In a guest essay published in today's New York Times, Lourd writes, "The Senate and House should move quickly and deliver the bill to President Trump for signature. That would ensure Americans retain control of their images and voices in the A.I. era."

The No Fakes Act was approved unanimously by the Senate Judiciary Committee in June, and, Lourd contends, there "is momentum to pass it through the full Congress before the end of the year." He calles it "one of the few A.I. bills with true bipartisan support." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

Hollywood, Lourd writes, "is not afraid of new technology."

"The objection from actors, musicians and other creators is to a world in which anyone can use their face or voice without permission," he writes. "In fact, many artists are already embracing A.I. on their own terms. Some of them are making deals with companies that are creating their A.I. likenesses, with their consent."

Lourd poses the issue as not just for Hollywood. "A content creator learned on her honeymoon that a YouTube ad was using an A.I. version of her to sell erectile dysfunction supplements," he writes. "Is all this legal? Right now, it’s an open question. But it shouldn’t be."

"Hollywood doesn’t need America’s leaders to devise a new concept for new circumstances," writes the chief executive and co-chairman of Creative Artists Agency. "We need them to extend and enforce the rules that already exist. The use of Americans’ faces, voices, performances and creative works is already subject to rules at the federal or state level that say, in short: You need to get permission, and you need to pay for the use."

"This principle has guided the entertainment industry for more than a century," he continues. "Whether it can continue to protect Americans may be decided in the coming weeks. The No Fakes Act would create a federal prohibition on creating nonconsensual digital replicas of any person’s voice or likeness — famous or not." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The No Fakes Act, Lourd says, "would apply a tried-and-true formula to the A.I. era: control, consent and compensation. It would set a uniform federal standard to replace outdated, ill-fitting state laws, many of them written with an analog world in mind. Its supporters include all sides of the table: SAG-AFTRA, the union representing actors and other performers; the Motion Picture Association, representing the studios; and tech companies including IBM, Google and OpenAI."

Earlier this month, Lourd told Deadline's Dominic Patten, that the issues around AI are "about the fundamental relationship between technological progress and creative rights, and who determines the value of creative work, who decides how that work is used, and whether creators will share in the opportunities AI creates."

articles.title: Doomsday Video Puts Fans In Thor, Beast, and More’s First Person POV
articles.summary: Marvel Studios If Marvel Studios can ever be accused of anything, it would be that it will never turn down an opportunity to go in an interesting direction with marketing—especially when it's marketing what looks like its biggest film yet: Avengers: Doomsday. Now the studio is teaming up with a surprising partner to put fans in the […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google If Marvel Studios can ever be accused of anything, it would be that it will never turn down an opportunity to go in an interesting direction with marketing—especially when it's marketing what looks like its biggest film yet: Avengers: Doomsday . Now the studio is teaming up with a surprising partner to put fans in the first-person POV of a few characters. In this new Visa ad, fans step into the shoes of Thor, Gambit, Beast, and The Thing as they navigate what seems like their everyday lives—cruising the Bifrost, getting flowers, ordering hair pomade, and having their rougher edges sanded down.

While the first-person POV was a nice change of pace from the usual advertising fare , Marvel Studios partnering with seemingly random businesses to promote its newest movie isn't a new tactic; they recently teamed up with the MLB during the World Series to run a TV spot with a few crumbs of new footage —and fans weren't particularly impressed. There was also another TV spot , this one standing on its own, that added a few sprinkles of never-before-seen moments to the conversation, including Doom performing some sort of magic while Drax looks at a sky that appears to be exploding in fire, Mystique morphing into Yelena, and Shuri and M’Baku meeting with Ben Grimm in a desert landscape.

A brand new Visa commercial features characters from ‘AVENGERS: DOOMSDAY’, including Thor, Gambit, Beast and The Thing. pic.twitter.com/m8oL6SEo5g

It's no secret that fans have been less than impressed with how Marvel has handled the marketing for Doomsday up to this point. With promised teaser trailers that never seemed to arrive, recycled content that showed the same 10 seconds of footage over and over, and a constant leaning into the joke that Steve Rogers is still Captain America, it seemed like audiences were in a content drought despite being so close to the film's release . And while the new Visa ad has a fun, casual vibe to it, it's obvious that Marvel has no interest in revealing anything new about the upcoming movie.

“This is the 10th f*cking time I’ve seen Doom stopping the Stormbreaker with his fingers,” said one fan. Another added, “And we are still not getting a real trailer. Two months to go," said one fan after the MLB spot. After the standalone TV spot, another said, "'New teaser’ and it’s rewarmed nachos.” So while there's no doubt that theaters will be filled to bursting on December 18th when Avengers: Doomsday drops, there's going to continue to be grumbling about the way that the movie was marketed and how Marvel handles its film marketing in general (we can choose to collectively forget the time when the Russo Brothers were their own surprise guests and a Doom-inspired cafe).

In the case of one game, this means that rather than its normal $60 price point, it is available for just $3. All of the deals come courtesy of the Xbox Store and are only available until December 1. After this, the AAA first-person shooter series will be priced like a AAA first-person shooter series rather than a bargain-bin steal.

The first-person shooter series in question is DICE and EA's military series, Battlefield , which, after a disappointing run, finally bounced back last year with the release of Battlefield 6 , one of the best games in the long-running franchise to date. And Battlefield 6 is on sale, but not at the prices of the rest of the series. It's been discounted by 67%, though, which drops its price from $70 to $23.09. The installment right before it, meanwhile, is 95% off on the Xbox Store, which means $2.99 rather than $60. Joining it are discounts that drop Battlefield 1 to $0.99, Battlefield 5 to $1.97, and Battlefield 4 to $0.99. There are also the same 95% discounts on various special editions for each game for those who want to pay a little extra for all the add-on goodies.

Battlefield 2042 and Battlefield 4 don't have a very active player base. You can find games, but it's not the most robust active player base. The latter is simply because of age, and the former is because it is the worst Battlefield game of all time. Battlefield 5 , meanwhile, has more active players than both, and is worth checking out in 2026 if you like World War 2, in particular. The most robust player base in 2026, other than Battlefield 6, is Battlefield 1 , one of the best games in the series, and the series' most recent take on World War I .

As you would expect, these are either the lowest prices ever for these various games or match the previous lowest prices, and they are unlikely to ever get much cheaper, as there isn't much gap between 95% off and simply giving the games away for free. The only way they could really get cheaper is through price reductions to the normal MSRP. In the case of something like Battlefield 2042 , which is still $60, this will happen, but with the older games, they have already been marked down to $20, and they are unlikely to be made any cheaper than this beyond sales.

If these particular deals don't tickle your fancy, there is a metric ton available on the Xbox Store, with more to be added for Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Meanwhile, a trio of N64 games is now available for free for some Xbox Series X users .

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Star Wars made its full anime series debut with a major Star Wars: Visions spin off hitting earlier this Summer, and the creator behind it revealed how there were some surprising complications when developing the series under Lucasfilm. Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi expanded on the original shorts seen in the anthology into a full series offering a whole new take on the Star Wars timeline. But while the production team had full freedom with the shorts, it turns out the situation was much different for the series.

Kenji Kamiyama, the director behind Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi and many other legendary anime releases , spoke about working on the series during 2nd Aichi-Nagoya International Animation Film Festival ( as spotted by Comic Book Resources ), and explained that he came across some surprising trouble with Lucasfilm when expanding on the shorts into a full work, "At first, I was told I could make it freely, but as it became a series, unique rules suddenly came out and Lucasfilm got angry at me."

But while Kamiyama noted a difficulty working with Lucasfilm over turning the shorts into a full series, it seems that the creative process ended up working out in a way that Kamiyama had been satisfied with, "It all started when I first wanted to make Star Wars , so I was genuinely happy to be working with those people, and at the same time, I wanted to test whether what I had been doing would be accepted by the people I admired, so I'm glad that I was able to achieve that." It all seems to have worked for Disney as well.

Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi released with Disney+ earlier this Summer as a limited series, but those behind the scenes have teased it would be possible to bring it back for a second season. At the very least, the spinoff has now opened the doors for potentially more of the shorts from Star Wars: Visions to get their own spinoffs in the future as well. Considering the critical success of this first outing , it's very much possible as Disney is always seeking out new Star Wars projects.

Star Wars: Visions Presents - The Ninth Jedi director Kenji Kamiyama also expressed a desire to continue the series with a potential second season . Although it was released as an eight episode limited series, the production team realized as they wrote out the episodes that there's potentially much more of the story to tell. Given how it also takes place at a far off version of the timeline, there's plenty of room to expand on the Star Wars universe lore as a whole.

Star Wars: Visions has been proof positive that Star Wars is a perfect fit for anime through the lens of all sorts of creators and their respective stories, and this new spinoff has been the strongest example of this yet. If you wanted to check it out along with the three seasons of the anthology series, you can now catch up with it all now streaming with Disney+ in the meantime. What did you think of The Ninth Jedi ? Would you want to see it return for Season 2? Let us know all of your thoughts about it in the comments.

Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Comic books are a special medium. Also called graphic novels, these books combine art and words to create something new that combines the greatest elements of both and generates something truly unique. When the medium is on full display, it can craft stories that couldn't exist anywhere else, but that doesn't mean that incredibly talented people haven't tried. Occasionally, a comic book becomes so beloved that people want to dig even deeper into it than the comic allowed, so the graphic novel is adapted into a traditional novel. There's always something lost in translation, but there's also a whole lot to gain in this jump. Today, we're looking at five novelizations of Marvel and DC comics and dissecting exactly what makes them so good and, depending on who you ask, even better than the stories they were based on.

This classic five-issue miniseries was adapted into a 283-page novel, exploring Matt's childhood and transition into the man who would become Daredevil. Just like Miller's foundational work, this novel takes us through Matt's life, exploring the various influences that forged him into the man he is . From his complicated but loving relationship with his father to his passionate connection with Elektra, everything is here, but they are dove into with new depth and time. The greatest things about this novel, easily, are the additional scenes and lingering moments that focus on how each character feels and their reasoning for what they do.

In his prime, Miller was a master of saying everything he needed to about a character without digging into the emotions themselves. He had a less-is-more style that showed rather than told the important emotions, leaving that mostly to the art. When it works, it works very well, but his work tends to come off as distant because of it. This novel, however, spends pages examining how each important moment affects Matt and others. It was a treat to slow down and sit in Battlin' Jack's resentment of how his life turned out, making every moment with him hit even harder. Matt's inner struggles are so much more vivid, as this book knows exactly when restraint is necessary, as well.

This novel adapted not just the classic "Death of Superman" story, but also its two immediate follow-ups in "Funeral for a Friend" and "Reign of the Superman," detailing the Man of Steel's death and return to save the day once again. Of course, this book was also written by the legendary Roger Stern, who also helped pen the original comic this was based on. That gave him a unique perspective that elevates this book by leaps and bounds, as Stern knew exactly what to focus on. This novelization was effectively a chance to retell this story as it felt to him, not just as the comic books demanded it must be formatted.

The most obvious example is in how it began, as chapter one kicks off with Superman saving John Henry Irons, which wouldn't be revealed until much later in the comics, which aimed to keep the mystery of the four Supermen alive. It's that kind of focus that places heart at the front of this adaptation. It knows exactly what made the comic work and hones in on those moments, all while also doing an incredible job of condensing and introducing necessary comic book lore in a way that any new reader could pick this book off the shelf and understand it. This work places the heart of the story before everything else, with a clear love for the source material, and that shines through to create an adaptation that makes us live the story in a new but equally delightful way, focused on emotions instead of the novelty of Superman being dead.

The "Civil War" event is one of Marvel's events that gets looked at less favorably with each passing year, but there's no denying that the impact it had was massive , nor that it's an idea that you can't help but let ruminate around in your head. This novel understands that the premise of Captain America and Iron Man standing on opposite ends of this conflict is easily the most interesting part of this event, and it takes that in stride, spending a wonderful amount of time in each character's head. The strongest parts of this novel, easily, are when we see the motivations that drive both men and push them farther and farther apart.

This novel also fundamentally establishes that this is different from the comic, bringing both the sliding timescale and retcons into account. The events were moved up to the year the book was released, setting it during Barack Obama's presidency instead of George W. Bush's, and even depicting Spider-Man post "One More Day" changes, meaning that he never married Mary Jane. It's a wonderful look into what "Civil War" would have looked like to the heroes at that time. I'll admit some bias for it, at least, given that I flipped through a few pages while I was a kid, and the description of Spider-Man's battle against Iron Man as Tony chased him into the sewers has stuck with me ever since.

"Days of Future Past" is one of the X-Men's most important storylines, and despite the fact that it's just two issues long, it was adapted into a 254-page novel. The obvious question is where all of that extra content came from, and it emerged from a combination of exploring everything added to the original story after the fact and taking it in its own direction. "Days of Future Past" has a truly inordinate number of sequels, and this novel draws most directly on the expanded history Rachel Summers wouldn't get till far after the original comic. Her perspective, absent from the comic, adds interesting contrast and context, but the biggest change is the inclusion of Kitty Pryde waking up in her older body.

In the comic, Kitty was simply replaced by her older self, but the novel had them switch places. Chapters alternated between Kate trying to guide her friends towards stopping the apocalypse, and Kitty living a waking nightmare where the world she was still learning how to save was falling apart. The added perspective gives the story a ton of extra content to explore, and the jump between characterizations is wonderful. Kate and Colossus's conversation before she travels to the past was especially wonderful, with even the add-ons capturing Peter's voice perfectly.

Just as with The Death and Life of Superman , this iconic Batman story was adapted by one of the many minds behind it, Greg Rucka. Of course, this is a special case, as this is the one novelization that actually cut far more content than it added. "No Man's Land" was a year-long status quo change that was told across a hundred issues, and no single novel could cover everything and do them all justice. Instead, this adaptation glossed over most of the day-by-day activities, instead honing in on the largest emotional beats, such as Hutnress's development, while replacing what it removed with dives into the characters the original focused too little on.

The big winners here are Renee Montoya, Cassandra Cain, and Harley Quinn. Renee's dynamic with Two-Face is explored and built like nowhere else here, serving as a fantastic dive into both of their psyches. It also gave extra context to Harley's introduction to the comics, given that this is where she hopped over from the cartoon. My personal favorite was definitely the extra attention given to Cass before her debut in the comics . Most of "No Man's Land" seems to lead up to her debut, but she wasn't seen until two issues before she became Batgirl. This novel takes the time to explore who she is, what she did, and how she fits into Gotham.

I could honestly go on about this novel all day. It doesn't have the scale that makes the original comic so captivating and addictive, but it knows exactly what emotional beats need to build towards the fantastic moments that made the comic work. The opening chapters told from Barbara's perspective are downright beautiful, and I was on the edge of my seat, even though I knew everything that was coming. I definitely recommend checking this out if you get the chance.

Which novelization of a comic do you think captures the spirit of the original the most? Let us know your personal favorite in the comments below!

articles.title: I Found Out From The Director and Mckenna Grace My Favorite Sunrise On The Reaping Scene WAS Shot, But Cut
articles.summary: What bummer, but I get it.
articles.content:
Minor spoilers ahead for The Hunger Games : Sunrise on the Reaping .

I loved the S unrise on the Reaping book , and was wildly impressed by how well it was adapted for film. Unfortunately, the scene where Maysilee kills a Gamemaker alongside District 4 career Maritte didn't make it. As you can see in the video above, I asked Francis Lawrence about this decision, where he confirmed the sequence was shot during principal photography. In his words:

Points were made. While it would have been awesome to see Maysilee kill a Gamemaker, in the novel it's connected to her relationship with Haymitch. They have an argument afterward about him still implicitly submitting to The Capitol, and not killing the Gamemakers despite being the closest Tribute to them. As director Francis Lawrence told me, that confrontation between the District 12 tributes didn't make sense for the movie adaptation, especially after following Joseph Zada's protagonist as he attempted to break The Arena.

Fingers crossed that we get to see this scene sometime in the future, via special features when the latest Hunger Games prequel is released to homes. This isn't the only change made to Sunrise on the Reaping , which included some references to Lucy Gray Baird from Songbirds and Snakes . Of course, I had to ask the actress who brought Maysilee to life about the cut sequence.

While interviewing the cast of the new Hunger Games movie, I asked Mckenna Grace about Maysilee's cut scene. She spoke about the argument with Joseph Zada's Haymitch that followed the Gamemaker death, telling me:

Points were made. As awesome as it would have been to see Maysilee kill a Gamemaker with one of her poisoned darts, that sequence also complicated her relationship with Haymitch shortly before her death. Instead, Francis Lawrence and company decided to keep the District 12 tributes as a united force until Mckenna Grace's character was killed by bird mutts. As such, the death and Haymitch's reaction are given extra emotional weight.
